title: Overthinking Is Exhausting
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Rumination is treated here as a leadership defect with a behavioural cure. The author starts from the common belief that more deliberation yields better outcomes, then argues that what deliberation actually produces past a certain point is self-doubt, anxiety and a manufactured need to keep going. The sharpest formulation defines overthinking as the art of addressing problems that don't exist: turning an issue over repeatedly magnifies every flaw until minor cracks acquire an importance they never had, and there is always another rock to turn over. Two practical moves follow. The first is detection — the signature is anxiety about a decision combined with fixation on the worst case. The second is the remedy: because overthinking is a failure to be solution-focused, any action that addresses the problem interrupts the loop, and even small steps can shake a leader loose. The piece notes that action-orientation is usually a leader's native strength, abandoned rather than absent, and closes on a borrowed aphorism that overthinking is the product of underdoing.
points: The diagnostic test offered is specific enough to use: anxiety about a decision plus fixation on the worst-case scenario means you are overthinking, not analysing.
The author's core distinction is between dwelling on a problem and all its parts versus examining options for a workable solution — the same hours spent very differently.
Overthinking is framed as self-inflicted rather than imposed: it generates the doubt and the additional work it then tries to resolve.
The cure is deliberately low-bar — any movement toward a solution breaks the spell, because occupying the mind with execution leaves less room for the problem.
Leaders are said to abandon an existing strength rather than lack one, which makes the fix a matter of returning to type.
quotes: We believe that by spending more time evaluating every option, turn, or nuance of a consequential problem we can bring it to a more successful outcome.

Essentially, overthinking is the art of addressing problems that don’t exist. Whenever we turn a problem over and over in the mind, we see every pitfall, crack, and blemish, making them larger and more important than they really are.
Any time you find yourself feeling worried or anxious over a decision or issue and at the same time fixating on the worst-case scenario, you are likely overthinking.
When we overthink, we dwell on the problem and all its parts. When problem-solving, we focus on examining options and finding a workable solution.
Good leaders are naturally action-oriented, but abandon this strength when they unintentionally choose to overthink.
Occupying the mind by executing an action prevents becoming consumed with the problem.
As one thinker puts it, overthinking is often the product of underdoing.
